faq.a: Statins robustly lower LDL‑C, the main driver of atherosclerosis, and have proven outcome data; fibrates mainly lower triglycerides.
faq.q: Why are statins preferred over fibrates for most patients?

faq.a: Yes for LDL‑C and total cholesterol; if triglycerides are > 2.3 mmol/L, obtain a fasting sample.
faq.q: Can I rely on a non‑fasting lipid profile?

faq.a: Only when clinical criteria are unclear or for cascade screening; it does not change immediate management.
faq.q: When is genetic testing for familial hypercholesterolaemia necessary?

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with HIV on protease inhibitors presents with LDL‑C 4.5 mmol/L; what is the next step? — Assess cardiovascular risk, optimise diet, and start a statin; consider drug‑interaction with protease inhibitors.

A patient with triglycerides 12 mmol/L develops acute epigastric pain; what distinguishes pancreatitis from other abdominal causes? — Serum amylase/lipase elevation and imaging; treat with insulin infusion and fibrates, avoid high‑fat meals.
How would you differentiate familial hypercholesterolaemia from diet‑induced hypercholesterolaemia? — Look for tendon xanthomas, family history of premature CAD, LDL‑C > 5 mmol/L despite normal diet.
In a low‑resource clinic without lipid labs, how do you estimate cardiovascular risk? — Use WHO/ISH risk charts based on age, sex, blood pressure, smoking, and diabetes status.

Why is ezetimibe added after maximal statin therapy rather than switching to a higher‑dose statin? — It provides additional LDL‑C reduction with fewer side‑effects and avoids high‑dose statin toxicity.
What red‑flag symptom in a patient with known dyslipidaemia mandates urgent referral? — New chest pain, dyspnoea, or neurological deficit suggesting acute coronary syndrome or stroke.
A pregnant woman has high triglycerides; which lipid‑lowering drug is contraindicated and why? — Statins are contraindicated due to teratogenic risk; manage with diet and omega‑3 fatty acids.
How does chronic kidney disease modify lipid‑lowering therapy? — Statins are first‑line; avoid fibrates in advanced CKD due to risk of rhabdomyolysis.
ai.title: Lipid Disorders
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Lipid disorders are abnormalities of serum cholesterol, triglycerides, or lipoproteins that increase cardiovascular risk. Diagnosis relies on a lipid profile and clinical context, especially in low‑resource settings where secondary causes are common.

b: Total cholesterol ≥ 5.2 mmol/L (200 mg/dL)
LDL‑C ≥ 3.0 mmol/L (115 mg/dL) for moderate risk, ≥ 4.1 mmol/L (160 mg/dL) for high risk
HDL‑C < 1.0 mmol/L (40 mg/dL) in men, < 1.2 mmol/L (45 mg/dL) in women
Triglycerides ≥ 1.7 mmol/L (150 mg/dL)
sections.p: Abnormal concentrations of total cholesterol, LDL‑C, HDL‑C, or triglycerides on a fasting lipid profile. Diagnosis uses the 2023 ESC/ACC thresholds.

t.b: What are the baseline lipid levels? – Confirms type and severity of dyslipidaemia.
What are the lipid levels when fasting not feasible? – Gives approximate LDL‑C; if triglycerides > 2.3 mmol/L, repeat fasting sample.

b: Very high risk: established ASCVD, LDL‑C ≥ 1.8 mmol/L
High risk: diabetes ≥ 40 yrs, moderate CKD, LDL‑C ≥ 2.6 mmol/L
Moderate risk: 10‑yr ASCVD risk 10‑20 %, LDL‑C 2.6‑3.5 mmol/L
Low risk: 10‑yr ASCVD risk < 10 %, LDL‑C < 2.6 mmol/L
sections.p: Risk‑based staging (low, moderate, high, very high) integrates lipid values with age, blood pressure, smoking, diabetes and existing CVD.

b: Diet high in saturated fat and refined carbs (common in urban East Africa)
HIV infection and protease‑inhibitor therapy
Tuberculosis treatment (rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes)
Chronic kidney disease
Familial hypercholesterolaemia (autosomal dominant)
Hypothyroidism
Nephrotic syndrome
sections.p: Identify secondary contributors before labeling primary genetic dyslipidaemia.

b: Incidental elevated cholesterol on routine labs
Xanthomas on tendons or extensor surfaces (familial hypercholesterolaemia)
Acute epigastric pain with triglycerides > 11.3 mmol/L (1000 mg/dL) – pancreatitis
Premature coronary artery disease
sections.p: Often asymptomatic; may be discovered during routine screening or after a cardiovascular event. Rarely, severe hypertriglyceridaemia causes pancreatitis.
Use a stepwise approach, adapting to test availability.

t.b: What are the exact lipid fractions? – Guides classification and treatment.
Is diabetes contributing? – Diabetes warrants tighter LDL‑C targets.
Is hypothyroidism present? – Treating thyroid disease can improve lipids.
Is renal disease a factor? – CKD influences drug choice and risk stratification.
Is familial hypercholesterolaemia likely? – Confirms diagnosis; not essential for management in low‑resource settings.
What alternative can be used? – Use point‑of‑care cholesterol meter or rely on clinical risk scores (e.g., WHO/ISH charts).

b: Acute pancreatitis with severe hypertriglyceridaemia
Sudden cardiac chest pain or dyspnoea – possible MI
Rapidly progressive xanthomas suggesting homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia
Lifestyle: diet low in saturated fat, increase fibre, regular aerobic activity, weight control, smoking cessation
Statins (e.g., simvastatin, atorvastatin) – first‑line for LDL‑C reduction; avoid in active liver disease
Ezetimibe – add if LDL‑C target not reached on maximal statin; cheap alternative to PCSK9 inhibitors
Fibrates (e.g., gemfibrozil) – for severe hypertriglyceridaemia; avoid with statins if risk of myopathy
Niacin – rarely used; limited benefit, can worsen hyperuricaemia
Counselling on adherence and monitoring for hepatic transaminase rise
sections.p: Treat reversible causes, then initiate lipid‑lowering therapy tailored to risk and resource availability.

b: Repeat lipid profile 4‑6 weeks after initiating/modifying therapy, then every 6‑12 months
Assess adherence, diet, and side‑effects at each visit
Use WHO/ISH risk charts for ongoing cardiovascular risk assessment
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus – reduces CVD events
sections.p: Regular monitoring ensures targets are met and complications are avoided.

b: Hypertriglyceridaemia secondary to uncontrolled diabetes – treat glucose first
Hypothyroidism‑induced hypercholesterolaemia – treat thyroid disease
Alcohol‑related triglyceride rise – address alcohol use
sections.p: Conditions that mimic dyslipidaemia clinically or biochemically.

b: Non‑fasting samples may overestimate triglycerides; confirm with fasting if > 2.3 mmol/L
Acute illness can lower LDL‑C temporarily – repeat after recovery
Laboratory interference from hemolysis can falsely raise triglycerides

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain or shortness of breath suggesting myocardial infarction
Severe abdominal pain with vomiting – possible pancreatitis
Sudden onset of neurological deficits – consider stroke in high‑risk dyslipidaemia
